ppt-webdev-css-001.pdfWording:
“Cascade” means CSS reads your rules and stacks them up, then decides which one “wins” when two rules target the same element. Three factors settle the fight, in this order:
Importance
Specificity
Source order

ppt-webdev-css-002.pdfWording: an ID selector is simply more specific than a class or an element selector, so it wins regardless of order.

Specificity
More specific selectors (ID > class > tag) win
Source order
If it's a tie, the rule written last wins

ppt-webdev-html-065.pdfWording:
HTML forms are the primary tool used by websites to collect data and input from visitors. Without them, the internet would be a one-way street where you could only read content rather than actively participate.
Forms bridge the gap between user interaction and backend processing, turning static web pages into interactive, dynamic applications.
ppt-webdev-html-065.clarification: HTML forms collect and submit data; safe handling also requires server-side validation and appropriate transport/output handling.

ppt-webdev-html-067.pdfWording: The wrapper or container for the entire form. It groups all the inputs and buttons together so the browser knows they belong to the same interactive section.

ppt-webdev-html-068.pdfWording: The text caption for a specific input field. In your code, the for="name" attribute links it directly to the input with id="name". This tells screen readers exactly what the input is for and allows users to click the text to focus on the input field.

ppt-webdev-html-069.pdfWording: The interactive field where a user types or selects data. The attribute type="text" specifically turns it into a single-line text box.

ppt-webdev-html-070.pdfWording: The clickable element used to trigger an action. Setting type="submit" tells the browser to process and send the form's collected data when clicked.

ppt-webdev-html-071.pdfWording:
<input type="text">
<input type="password">
<input type="email">
<input type="number">
<input type="date">
<input type="radio">
<input type="checkbox">
<input type="file">
<input type="submit">

ppt-webdev-html-072.pdfWording: Use for general, single-line text inputs that don't fit into a specialized category. Examples include names, usernames, or search terms.

ppt-webdev-html-073.pdfWording: Use whenever a user types sensitive credentials. The browser automatically masks the characters with dots or stars to protect them from onlookers.
ppt-webdev-html-073.clarification: Masking password characters hides them from onlookers; it does not encrypt the submitted value.

ppt-webdev-html-074.pdfWording: Use specifically for gathering email addresses. It forces the browser to validate that the text follows a standard format (e.g., contains an "@") and pulls up an optimized keyboard on mobile devices.
ppt-webdev-html-074.clarification: Email input checks syntax, not whether an address exists. Required fields still need the required attribute, and server-side validation remains necessary.

ppt-webdev-html-075.pdfWording: Use when you need numerical entries, such as quantities or ages. It rejects non-numeric characters and often provides small arrow buttons to increment or decrement the value.
ppt-webdev-html-075.clarification: Browser controls differ; client-side number constraints do not replace server-side validation.

ppt-webdev-html-076.pdfWording: Use for scheduling or selecting specific calendar dates. It opens a standardized native calendar picker widget tailored to the user's browser or device.

ppt-webdev-html-077.pdfWording: Use when a user must pick exactly one option from a predefined group (e.g., choosing a shipping method). Selecting one will automatically deselect any other option in that group.
ppt-webdev-html-077.clarification: Radio buttons form a group using the same name; selecting one deselects the other buttons in that group.

ppt-webdev-html-078.pdfWording: Use when a user can select multiple options from a list, or for a single binary choice (e.g., agreeing to terms of service).

ppt-webdev-html-079.pdfWording: Use when the user needs to upload something from their local device memory, such as photos, documents, or spreadsheets.

ppt-webdev-html-080.pdfWording: Use to create the button that packages all the filled-out form data and sends it over to the server for processing.

ppt-webdev-html-082.pdfWording: Creates a large, multi-line box where users can type long messages or paragraphs.

ppt-webdev-html-083.pdfWording: Creates a clickable button that sends the filled-out form data to a server or web page action.

ppt-webdev-html-084.pdfWording: Creates a drop-down menu. The <select> tag is the container, and each <option> tag inside it is a choice the user can pick, like "Philippines" or "Japan".

ppt-webdev-html-086.pdfWording: action: Specifies the URL or file path where the form's data should be sent when submitted.

ppt-webdev-html-087.pdfWording: method: Defines the HTTP method (typically GET or POST) used to send the form data to the server.

ppt-webdev-html-088.pdfWording: name: Assigns a unique identifier to the element, which is used as the key when sending the form data to the server.
ppt-webdev-html-088.clarification: Form controls can share a name (for example a radio group). A name is a submission key and is not required to be unique.

ppt-webdev-html-089.pdfWording: id: Provides a completely unique identifier for the element across the entire web page, primarily used for styling with CSS or targeting with JavaScript.
ppt-webdev-html-089.clarification: IDs should be unique and are also used for label associations and fragment links, not only styling or JavaScript.

ppt-webdev-html-090.pdfWording: value: Sets the initial or current content inside an input field.

ppt-webdev-html-091.pdfWording: placeholder: Displays a faint, temporary hint or example text inside an empty input field before the user starts typing.

ppt-webdev-html-092.pdfWording: required: Forces the user to fill out or select the field before they are allowed to submit the form.

ppt-webdev-html-093.pdfWording: disabled: Shuts down the element so the user cannot interact with it, and prevents its value from being submitted with the form.

ppt-webdev-html-094.pdfWording: readonly: Allows the user to see and select the text inside a field but prevents them from changing it, while still allowing the value to be submitted.

ppt-webdev-html-095.pdfWording:

Ensures a field cannot be left blank before submission.

Sets lower and upper numeric or date limits for number/range/date inputs.
pattern
Restricts text to letters only (uppercase and lowercase) using a regular expression pattern.

Restricts the minimum and maximum character lengths for text strings.
type="email"
Automatically validates that the entered text follows a standard email format
ppt-webdev-html-095.clarification: The letters-only restriction comes from the particular [A-Za-z]+ pattern shown in the slide; pattern validation can express other rules.

ppt-webdev-html-096.pdfWording: Ensures a field cannot be left blank before submission.

ppt-webdev-html-098.pdfWording: Restricts text to letters only (uppercase and lowercase) using a regular expression pattern.
ppt-webdev-html-098.clarification: This describes the slide’s specific [A-Za-z]+ example, not every possible pattern value.

ppt-webdev-html-099.pdfWording: Restricts the minimum and maximum character lengths for text strings.

ppt-webdev-html-100.pdfWording: Automatically validates that the entered text follows a standard email format
ppt-webdev-html-100.clarification: This is a syntax check. It does not establish that the email address exists or can receive messages.

ppt-webdev-html-101.pdfWording:
HTML5 provide basic client-side validation without JavaScript by using declarative attributes and semantic input types directly in markup, eliminating the need for JavaScript for standard checks.
When a user submits a form, the browser automatically checks the input elements against specified constraint rules. If any field fails validation, the browser blocks submission and displays a native error bubble.
ppt-webdev-html-101.clarification: The source says “HTML5 provide.” Client-side validation can be bypassed and is not a replacement for server-side validation.

ppt-webdev-html-103.pdfWording: Web Accessibility refers to the design and development of websites that can be accessed, understood, navigated, and used by all individuals, including persons with disabilities.

ppt-webdev-html-104.pdfWording:
Ensures equal access to online information and services.
Provides a more inclusive and usable web experience.
Supports users with different abilities and needs.
Enables compatibility with assistive technologies.

ppt-webdev-html-105.pdfWording:

ppt-webdev-html-107.pdfWording: Keyboard Accessibility - Websites should be fully navigable and operable using a keyboard.

ppt-webdev-html-108.pdfWording: Clear Content Structure - Content should be logically organized and presented in an understandable manner.

ppt-webdev-html-109.pdfWording: Meaningful Links - Link text should clearly indicate its destination or purpose.

ppt-webdev-html-110.pdfWording: Alternative Text - Meaningful images should have appropriate text descriptions.

ppt-webdev-html-111.pdfWording: Proper Headings - Headings should follow a logical hierarchy to organize page content.

ppt-webdev-html-112.pdfWording: Accessible Forms - Forms should provide clear labels, instructions, required fields, and error messages.

ppt-webdev-html-113.pdfWording: Text Readability and Contrast - Text should be sufficiently readable and have adequate contrast with its background.

ppt-webdev-html-114.pdfWording: Headings should be used to establish structure and meaning, not merely to increase the visual size of text.

ppt-webdev-html-115.pdfWording:
<h1> – identifies the main topic or title of the page.
<h2> – identifies major sections.
<h3> – identifies subsections under an <h2>.
<h4> to <h6> – provide additional levels of organization when necessary.

ppt-webdev-html-116.pdfWording: It is a textual description associated with an image that communicates its relevant purpose or meaning.
